newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges Congress to act on chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Congress to act on chemical treaty.

text.p: President Bill Clinton issued a strong appeal to Congress on Tuesday to ratify a global chemical weapons ban, saying: "We have no more important obligations."

Ratification of the Chemical Weapons Treaty is being held up mainly by the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Republican Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina, who wants several other security issues settled first.

Clinton, speaking in his annual State of the Union speech before Congress, called ratification of the treaty "a new test of leadership." He added: "It will make our troops safer from chemical attack. It will help us to fight terrorism."
The Clinton administration wants the Senate to approve the 1993 treaty by April 29. If Washington does not ratify it by then, it will have no say in administration of the ban.

"We have no more important obligations -- especially in the wake of what we now know about the Gulf War," Clinton said, referring to reports of contamination from Iraqi chemical weapons when U.S. forces blew up Iraqi bunkers.

He noted the treaty has had bipartisan backing from the start. It came close to being ratified by the Senate last year but was withdrawn before a vote after an erosion of Republican support associated with the presidential election campaign.
Earlier on Tuesday, the State Department rejected attempts by Helms to link ratification of the treaty to other issues such as foreign affairs restructuring and U.N. reform.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said new Secretary of State Madeleine Albright "strongly disagrees that these issues should be linked to Senate advice and consent to ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention."
"Each is an important issue ... that should be addressed on their own merits," Burns told a news briefing.
Helms on Monday urged Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott to focus on several other security-related issues before dealing with the treaty and called for a series of conditions to Senate approval.
As committee chairman, Helms has the power to prevent the treaty, which he says is deficient, from going to the Senate floor for ratification.
In a letter to Lott, he listed other priorities that he said should come first, saying that when they had become law, "We can turn our attention to the matter of the CWC."

On his list were legislation to fold three foreign affairs agencies into the State Department, reform of the United Nations, submitting modifications of two other arms treaties to the Senate and enacting legislation to deploy a national missile defence system.
Burns said Albright agreed with Helms that reorganizing foreign affairs agencies and U.N. reform were important issues on which she wanted to pursue a bipartisan approach.
But, he said, U.S. exclusion from administering the chemical weapons treaty "gets to our credibility and that affects negatively our leadership on a whole range of arms and proliferation issues."

The treaty bans production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons. The United States and Russia, which also has not ratified the pact, are the only two countries that admit holding chemical weapons stocks.
Burns said Albright already had visited Congress twice to discuss the pact since she was sworn in on Jan. 23 and planned to contact Helms again in the next few days on the issue.
